Can confirm the ordering, from the other side: I maintain a different hook-driven notch and had exactly this race, without realising it until I read this issue. `run_in_background: true` Bash reliably delivers its PostToolUse after Stop, and the fix wasn't specific to Bash.

What worked for me was making "turn ended" an absorbing state rather than adding an ordering assumption to the phase machine:

- on Stop, record the session id as finished
- drop PostToolUse for a session whose turn has finished
- clear that flag on UserPromptSubmit, or on the next PreToolUse

Those two events are the only ones that mean real new work has started, so a normal mid-turn PostToolUse still lands, and the next turn behaves normally. Allowing `.waitingForInput -> .processing` is then fine, because the late hook never reaches the transition.

Worth noting it generalises past background Bash: any hook that arrives after Stop for the same turn (a slow PostToolUse from a long-running tool, a late transcript read) will flip the state back, and there is nothing following it to correct the display because Claude is idle. Gating on "has this turn ended" catches all of them, where special-casing background Bash catches one.

I went down the same road recently and landed somewhere different that might be worth knowing about: instead of animating sprite frames, I rebuilt the character from its pixel grid and rig the parts. The artwork turned out to separate cleanly into a torso, two eyes, two arms and four legs, so the legs can take real steps, the eyes blink and track the cursor, and it can shut its eyes to sleep, all from the one image and no frame sheets.

Two things that mattered more than I expected:

Legs move in diagonal pairs, not left-pair then right-pair. That's what four-legged animals actually do, and it's the difference between a walk and a shuffle.

Limbs have to overlap into the body, with the body drawn last. Mine had the arms flush against the torso, turning about their inner edge, which opened a wedge of daylight at the shoulder on every swing.

The other lesson was pacing rather than animation. Mine appeared roughly a quarter of every idle minute at first, which is charming for ten minutes and maddening for an afternoon. Every activity now buys a silence proportional to its own length, so a long nap earns a long absence, and it's ambient again.

Mine is [ClaudeNotch](https://github.com/rawsun007/claude-notch), a separate app rather than a fork, but the pieces are standalone if you want to read them: [PetRig.swift](https://github.com/rawsun007/claude-notch/blob/main/Sources/ClaudeNotch/PetRig.swift) for the gait and limbs, [PetEngine.swift](https://github.com/rawsun007/claude-notch/blob/main/Sources/ClaudeNotch/PetEngine.swift) for the behaviour and pacing. Both pure functions, easy to lift.
